 Nebraska’s U.S. Senate race is drawing national attention as incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts seeks reelection against Independent Dan Osborn, America First candidate Chuck Conboy, and Nebraska Working People Party chair Robin Richards ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
 NTV spoke with Senator Ricketts, Osborn and Conboy on the state of the country, personal priorities and other key issues. Candidate Richards could not be reached for an interview.
 Asked whether he believes elections are secure and what he thinks about the possibility of armed federal agents being sent to polling places, Conboy said, “Until we have voter ID, we'll never have secure elections. We never have had. We never will” He added of armed federal agents at polling sites, “It sounds like the Gestapo to me. No, it's like everybody I talked to actually laughs about it. It's like 'Right, yeah, we need armed forces at the site.' We don't need armed forces to the sites. That's absolutely chaos.”
 Ricketts said states should run their own elections. “Every state should manage its own elections,” he said. “I will tell you, there's huge problems in other states. So for example, where you have a state that just mails out ballots, that just opens you up to election fraud.” He said he is confident however about Nebraska’s system: “I'm confident here in Nebraska we're good.”
 Osborn said he trusts the process and poll workers, and opposed the idea of armed agents at polling places. “I got to believe in the process, the poll, the polling stations and the fact that we have poll workers that volunteer from both sides of the aisle to protect our elections,” he said. “But armed troops at polling stations, that's not who America is. That's not a free country. That's that's probably what North Korea and China and Russia do. That's not who we are.”
 On political polarization and what they would do to lower tensions, Conboy said, “You know, what really killed this country is Covid. Covid divided this country and it was by design.” He criticized both major parties and argued for more independents in office, saying, "the Democrats and the Republicans in Congress are radical. You've got two independents in there and one of those is Bernie Sanders, but you have 'two' independents. We need a lot more until we can stop this nonsense of, 'yeah, you're Democrat or Republican, liberal or conservative.' Until we can stop that and say, 'no, I'm an American.' Until that comes back into vogue, we're in trouble. We need more independents."
 Ricketts pointed to Senate rules that often require bipartisan support. “Well, one of the great things about the US Senate is that most bills require 60 votes to get passed, which means both Republicans and Democrats have to participate,” he said. “And so if you look at just about any major legislation, it has both Republicans and Democrats that are contributing to it.”
 Osborn called polarization “unacceptable” and said he wants to build a broader coalition. “It's unacceptable. It's sad,” he said. “And what I'm trying to do about it is I'm trying to create a coalition. I talk to Democrats, Republicans, Libertarians, Legalized Marijuana Now, independents, you name it, trying to bring everybody together on the issues that we know we can agree on and and stop dividing us on the issues that we don't. ” Osborn added, “I think that's it's all by design to keep us divided. That's the art of the war, right? Divide and conquer. If you're successful at that, you can keep winning elections on your issues."
 When asked about a personal priority issue, Conboy focused on higher education costs and student debt, citing struggles faced by his own family. “Universities should be [at] an extremely reduced price Student debt is approaching...$2 trillion in this country,” he said. “That's a lot of money. 98% of that is held by the US government. That's ridiculous...I have friends that, 20 years down the road are still trying to pay off their student loans. That's absolutely ludicrous.”
 Ricketts said his personal priorities include lowering costs and supporting agriculture, pointing to the need for a new farm bill. “We're going to need to continue to focus on putting more money back in people's pockets and bringing down the cost of living,” he said. “We also need to continue to support agriculture.” Ricketts said passing a farm bill would provide “the certainty of a five year farm bill” for farmers and ranchers and said it would help lower grocery costs. He also cited E15 as something that “will also help bring down costs.”
 Osborn said one of his priorities is releasing the full Epstein files, with protections for victims. “Releasing the entirety of the Epstein files unredacted, except for protecting the names of the survivors and victims,” he said. “That has to be paramount when releasing those” Osborn added, “If you've trafficked underage women and you were a part of that, you should have your day in court and then you should go to jail. It doesn't matter if you're a prince, prime minister or president or a former president. It doesn't matter how much money you have.”
 Asked to say something nice about an opponent, Osborn said of Ricketts, “I mean, he's a he's a he's a good politician, right? I would say the level of fight that he has is pretty good. I don't like his brand of politics. But you know, not for a lack of trying there... He's got nice suits too."
 Ricketts praised Osborn’s military service: “Well, I always appreciate any anybody who serves our country as a veteran, and my opponent has served our country in the Navy. And I always appreciate what veterans do for our country. We have a free country because veterans step up to serve us."
 In final remarks, Conboy urged voters to stay engaged. “Please don't give up. Don't ever give up,” he said. "The United States of the greatest country in the world. People of Nebraska are the greatest people in that country. You deserve the best. And if I can't bring it to you for some reason, there is somebody out there that can. Don't settle for second best. Never settle."
 Ricketts said he has a record of service. “I've been delivering for Nebraskans for 12 years. You know where I stand. You know what I'll do,” he said. He added, “You may not agree with what I say, but you're always going to know where I'm going to stand because I'm going to tell it to you straight...with my opponent you're never going to know what he's going to say or what he's going to do, because he's been telling Nebraskans both."
 Osborn said he would base decisions on conversations with Nebraskans. “I think what you're going to get from me versus, you know, my opponent is you're going to get somebody who approaches their vote based off of the conversations I have here in Thedford and North Platte and wherever from the people that I talk to,” he said, “not based off of if defense contractors or AIPAC give me money.”
